justification: Formed a fresh judgment first, then checked round 1 and round 2 against the current text. Against the practical top-ranking pages (GeeksforGeeks, freeCodeCamp) this article remains clearly ahead: it is the only one of the three with worked (c, n0) witness constructions including a disproof, a from-scratch counting derivation of the running examples, and reproducible C# measurements (a crossover, a compiler-flag effect, a List-vs-HashSet comparison) instead of prose assertions or an external chart. Against Wikipedia, which has more pure-math breadth, it trades that for depth a reader can run and check. Both open round-2 findings are genuinely fixed, not just gestured at. (1) The Omega dual-convention claim (Hardy-Littlewood 1914 'infinitely often' vs. Knuth's 1976 'for all sufficiently large n') now has a real primary source in front matter -- Knuth, 'Big Omicron and Big Omega and Big Theta', ACM SIGACT News 8(2), 1976, linked via a text mirror -- cited inline at the exact sentence, including a direct quote. I independently verified the quote against Wikipedia's citation of the same paper and it matches ('For all the applications I have seen so far in computer science, a stronger requirement ... is much more appropriate.'), so this is a real, accurately quoted source, not a fabrication. (2) The no-Optimize crossover run is still prose-only and still not exercised by run-code.mjs, but the article now says so explicitly, names the exact reason (avoiding a second hundred-line paste of an unchanged harness), and points the reader back to the visible id=crossover block by id with a one-line reproduction recipe -- the alternative fix round 2 explicitly allowed, and it removes the earlier ambiguity about which program to rerun. I re-read the whole article fresh for new problems and found none worth listing: headings remain content-specific and do not repeat the boilerplate or heading patterns of sibling articles (amortized-analysis, arrays-and-dynamic-arrays) when their heading lists are placed side by side; the closing paragraph still names concrete next topics (recurrences/Master theorem, the wider sorting toolbox) rather than trailing off; docs/crosslinks/complexity/big-o-notation.md still exists and is sensible, with an explicit boundaries-with-siblings section that heads off near-duplicate coverage with the planned sorting-algorithms and analyzing-loops-and-recursion articles; every in-body internal link (three glossary anchors, /complexity/amortized-analysis/) resolves to a real entry, so there is no dead-end navigation. Web searches on five distinctive sentences and phrases (the opening race-timing scenario, 'the shape of the code, not a stopwatch, told you', the 'age 30 is under 90' analogy, the exact lap-counting phrasing, the Knuth quote itself) found no unattributed copying; the Knuth quote is the one intentional, properly cited quotation on the page. Held back from a clear 10: this is still an upper-intermediate reference page rather than something with a genuinely new angle beyond 'derive and measure what competitors assert', and one verifiability gap remains open by design (the unoptimized run is reproducible by a reader but not machine-checked by the site's own harness) -- narrow enough to be a nit, not a fault.
